analysis.one_liner: Narrows when two companies count as one employer for workers' union and wage protections.
analysis.headline: The House committee approved the bill 20-16 in July 2025, it was reported to the House on December 30, 2025, and the House adopted a rule on January 13, 2026 putting it on the floor; no final vote has happened yet.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, two companies can be treated as one employer when they share control over working conditions, which lets workers unionize across companies and sue both companies for unpaid wages. This bill says two companies count as one employer under the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act only if one company directly, actually, and immediately controls hiring, firing, pay, benefits, scheduling, day-to-day supervision, or discipline [S3]. The practical effect: a national fast-food chain or a hotel brand could keep setting the rules for its franchisees and contractors through contracts, without sharing legal responsibility when those workers are shorted on pay or blocked from unionizing.
analysis.who_benefits: National franchise chains, brands, and companies that control work through franchise or staffing contracts. They keep the ability to dictate prices, standards, and operations at local locations without being legally responsible as an employer for wage or union violations at those locations [S3]. Local franchise owners also gain, because they can no longer be pulled into joint-employer liability for decisions made by the parent brand.

how_it_helps.text: For union rights (National Labor Relations Act), a company is a joint employer only if it directly, actually, and immediately exercises significant control over hiring, firing, pay, benefits, scheduling, supervision, or discipline [S3].
The same standard applies to wage and hour rules under the Fair Labor Standards Act, which governs minimum wage and overtime claims [S2][S3].
Supporters, led by Rep. James Comer, frame this as protecting local franchise businesses from being held responsible for decisions made by a parent corporation [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Workers at franchised and subcontracted workplaces. If a company that effectively sets the terms of their job no longer counts as their employer, workers can face shorter leashes on organizing and, when a local employer goes broke or stiffs them on wages, they may have no one with money to sue. They also lose the leverage of bargaining with the big brand that actually sets their conditions.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets a dominant company keep control over essential terms of work through contract terms while escaping the legal duties of an employer, which shifts the cost of unpaid wages, retaliation, and union suppression onto workers [S3].

Critics of joint-employer liability argue the broader standard it replaces held franchisors responsible for day-to-day personnel decisions they do not actually make, and made it riskier to franchise or subcontract; this bill would restore that insulation and make it much harder for the National Labor Relations Board or courts to reach the company with real economic power.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real legal certainty and reduced liability for franchise owners and national brands, which is its stated purpose. The cost falls on workers in franchised and subcontracted workplaces: organizing and wage claims become harder to pursue against the company that actually sets the terms of the job. Because the legal standard still allows franchisors to direct franchisees through detailed contracts, the bill preserves the control that makes joint liability meaningful while removing the responsibility.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it 20-16, it was reported to the House floor at the end of December, and on January 13, 2026 the House passed a rule bringing it up for consideration; the full House vote has not yet happened and the Senate has not acted.

narrative.text: Rep. James Comer (R-KY) introduced the bill on July 14, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce [S1].
On July 23, 2025, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported by a vote of 20-16 [S5].
On December 30, 2025, the committee reported the bill as amended (H. Rept. 119-422) and it was placed on the Union Calendar [S2][S3][S5].

On January 12, 2026, the Rules Committee reported a rule (H. Res. 988) bundling this bill with four others, providing a closed rule (no floor amendments) for H.R. 4366; the House passed the rule on January 13, 2026 [S5].
The bill has only 2 cosponsors, both Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: If the House passes it as scheduled, national franchise brands and staffing firms come out ahead, gaining control without employer liability; workers in franchised workplaces come out behind. As of now, the outcome is still open in the Senate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Franchise chains, if enacted; outcome still open

sides.party_line_note: Every stage so far has run on party lines: the committee vote was 20-16 with all 16 no votes from Democrats, both cosponsors are Republicans, and the Republican majority used its floor-scheduling power to bring the bill up under a closed rule.

industries.industry: Franchise corporations (fast-food chains, hotel brands, retail franchises)
industries.note: They keep direct contractual control over the essential terms of work at franchise locations while no longer being legally responsible as an employer for wage or union violations there. The cost of that shield is borne by workers, who can reach only the local employer.

Companies that supply workers to a client site would count as the workers' sole employer unless the client directly and immediately controls essential terms, limiting wage-and-hour claims against the client company.

They shed the risk of being pulled into joint-employer liability for the parent brand's decisions, which supporters cite as the bill's core purpose. The trade-off is that workers shorted by a struggling franchisee can no longer recover from the well-capitalized brand.

A narrow joint-employer standard makes it much harder to bargain with, or file unfair labor practice claims against, the national company that actually sets conditions for franchise and contract workers.

analysis.trajectory: With a closed rule adopted on January 13, 2026, House passage looks likely given the Republican majority (223 of 440 voting members). The bill then faces the Senate, where the 55 Republicans would need 60 votes to cut off debate unless it moves through reconciliation; a bill of this kind has historically stalled there. If the House passes it and it dies in the Senate, the Congress ends with no change to the joint-employer standard.
